utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Please be seated. Have the accused brought in, please. (The accused entered court)

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Good afternoon to the interpreters and to everybody else who is involved in our hearing this afternoon. First of all, I would like to apologise, on behalf of the Trial Chamber, to the Office of the Prosecutor. They know that we would begin today at 2.00 and not at 5.00. Therefore, excuse us. The Defence was better informed than the Office of the Prosecutor, which shows that that can happen, you see. We're going to resume, and we have confidence in the Prosecution for cross-examination of the witness. If you have any problems, any slight problems, I say slight problems, if you have any problems at all, the Trial Chamber will try to take note of that. Is it Mr. Nobilo who is going to speak now?

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. The next witness will be testifying in open session, without any protective measures.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: All right. So that I can refer to your summary, would you tell us the name of the witness? Of course, I'll ask him to repeat it, but what is his name?

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: It is Mrs. Palic-Mitrecic Silvia. So her name is Silvia Palic-Mitrecic. (The witness entered court)

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Mr. Prosecutor, are you ready?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Do you hear me, Madam? Please remain standing. Tell us your name, your given names, your age, your profession, your last residence and then you will take an oath.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: My name is Silvia Palic-Mitrecic. I was born in 1956. I'm from Zagreb. I have graduated from the Political Science Faculty.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Do you still live in Zagreb?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I live in Zagreb.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Would you help the witness with her headset, please? That's better. Do you hear me? All right. You're going to take an oath now.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Thank you very much. You may be seated. You have agreed to testify in the trial at the International Criminal Tribunal for the former Yugoslavia, initiated by the Prosecutor, who is in the courtroom, against General Blaskic, who at the time was a Colonel, who is on your left. You're going to first testify by answering the questions of the party that asked you to come, the Defence, Mr. Nobilo. All right. Mr. Nobilo, proceed, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Examined by Mr. Nobilo:

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mrs. Palic, you said that you were born in 1956 in Zagreb and that you graduated from the Faculty of Political Science. Tell us, please, before the war broke out where were you employed?

utterances.speaker: SILVIA PALIC-MITRECIC
utterances.text: I worked in the school for health technicians as a professor there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: We're going to make breaks between the question and the answer for the benefit of our interpreters. At one point did you join, as volunteer, the Croatian army?

utterances.speaker: SILVIA PALIC-MITRECIC
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you tell us when that was and where you were, what duties you performed, what units you were a member of?

utterances.speaker: SILVIA PALIC-MITRECIC
utterances.text: In 1992, as a volunteer, I entered the Croatian army, the units of the Croatian army in the 153rd Brigade, and that was up to 1994. In 1994, in July, I went to the area of Zagreb as a counsellor. That is I went -- was in the independent reconnoitring unit, and up until 1995, that is to say, April of 1995, I was in the Zagreb area as counsellor for sports and culture.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You were in the Croatian army as a volunteer, and like many other women in Croatia you hold a rank?

utterances.speaker: SILVIA PALIC-MITRECIC
utterances.text: Yes, I am a Warrant Officer in the Croatian army.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What would the equivalent be in the JNA?

utterances.speaker: SILVIA PALIC-MITRECIC
utterances.text: It would be First Lieutenant.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Are you still in the Croatian army?

utterances.speaker: SILVIA PALIC-MITRECIC
utterances.text: No, I'm not.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you work somewhere privately or do you work for the state?

utterances.speaker: SILVIA PALIC-MITRECIC
utterances.text: I have my own company, and I work in that company.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: As we're going to see from your testimony, you organised a number of activities geared towards the so-called Bihac pocket or the Bosanska Krajina region of Western Bosnia. Could you describe to the Court how you began your work and what you duties you performed first?

utterances.speaker: SILVIA PALIC-MITRECIC
utterances.text: When I joined the Croatian army as a volunteer, I was given an assignment by my commanding officer to organise a humanitarian convoy, and to join the community of Croats and Muslims who would help me to organise that humanitarian convoy. Assistance in organising it itself was given to me by the students from Bosnia, Muslim students, and they were part of this Bosnian and Croat community, and they helped me to load and unload, and generally in the organisation of the humanitarian convoy.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you give us a date? When was this?

utterances.speaker: SILVIA PALIC-MITRECIC
utterances.text: It was in 1992, in May.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Your involvement, geared towards Western Bosnia, was -- is it finished with that convoy, or did it become something else, did it grow into something else?

utterances.speaker: SILVIA PALIC-MITRECIC
utterances.text: Yes, it grew into something else. First of all, the students expressed the desire in organising the humanitarian convoys to go to Bihac. Second, I was given an order by my commanding officer that I -- I was given the go-ahead to organise these young people and to send them to Bihac.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you said to organise and send to Bihac, what do you mean? How was this organised and why were you sending them to Bihac?

utterances.speaker: SILVIA PALIC-MITRECIC
utterances.text: Well, I collected up these young people, I sent them for military training, I equipped them, and then sent them there for the purpose of fighting, because there was a lot of fighting going on in the Bihac area at that time. There was an armed conflict going on.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And these young people, these students, were they mostly Muslims?

utterances.speaker: SILVIA PALIC-MITRECIC
utterances.text: Yes, mostly Muslims. That is to say, in that first group they were exclusively Muslims.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you describe the first group for the Court? When did you organise this first group and how did you train the first group, the first group of Muslims who were sent from Croatia to Bosnia, and when did that occur?

utterances.speaker: SILVIA PALIC-MITRECIC
utterances.text: The first group was made up of 23 young men, students, Muslims, and I talked to them first of all, I interviewed them and put them up at the barracks at Jastrebarsko belonging to the Croatian army, and the officers of the Croatian army, four of them, trained and prepared these young people. They were given complete sets of weapons from the Croatian army, whereas their uniforms and boots they obtained from the people they knew and who worked in Germany, Austria and so on. They would come in and organise fashion, buy this equipment and hand it over to these young people.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Once you had rallied them, how long did the training last?

utterances.speaker: SILVIA PALIC-MITRECIC
utterances.text: Well, as I say, I rallied them immediately after the first convoy left, and this was on the 20th of May. The first group was set up on the 20th of May. Training lasted approximately 25 to 30 days.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Where were they lodged? Was this at the expense of the Croatian army, and their food as well?

utterances.speaker: SILVIA PALIC-MITRECIC
utterances.text: Yes, everything was paid for by the Croatian army and everything took place in Jastrebarsko, the Croatian army barracks which was in the vicinity of Zagreb. Their lodging and food were paid for by the Croatian army.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So these 23 volunteers, these were all Muslims, were they not?

utterances.speaker: SILVIA PALIC-MITRECIC
utterances.text: Yes, they were.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How did you transport this group? Could you describe this for the benefit of the Trial Chamber, and how -- which territory did they have to pass through?

utterances.speaker: SILVIA PALIC-MITRECIC
utterances.text: While they were doing their training at the barracks, I contacted the commander of the student regiment of the Croatian army, and I asked them to send scouts to take over these young people and transport them to Bihac. The route from Slunja to Bihac is 105 kilometres, and it goes by Serbian territory, on foot.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did they perform their job properly?

utterances.speaker: SILVIA PALIC-MITRECIC
utterances.text: Yes, they did.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And these young men, the young men you organised, future members of the HVO and another five Muslims went with them; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SILVIA PALIC-MITRECIC
utterances.text: Yes. When talking to the commander of the Slunja regiment, I was given an order to include nine other individuals who were in the Slunja regiment itself and who were to go to Bihac, and I accepted these nine people. As I say, there were nine of them, and four or five were Muslims, the rest were Croats.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But the first group was not the last group. This was just the beginning. Could you describe how the second group was established and what you did and how you trained the second group?

utterances.speaker: SILVIA PALIC-MITRECIC
utterances.text: The second group was a much larger group. As I say, in addition to the 23 plus 9 men that the first group had, which is a total of 32, the second group numbered about 200 individuals, and they either came from other battlegrounds to Croatia, also as members of the Croatian army, where they were released from the Croatian army in order to be transferred to Bihac. These were all people from that part, from that region. Or they came on their own BAT. I took them in, organised them, once again with the help of my command, and I organised lodging for them, equipment, weapons and so on.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The Croatian soldiers who were released to go to -- to be able to go to Bosnia and the battleground there, were they Muslims?

utterances.speaker: SILVIA PALIC-MITRECIC
utterances.text: Yes, they were.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And they joined the Territorial Defence of Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: SILVIA PALIC-MITRECIC
utterances.text: Yes. Once they arrived in Bihac they joined the Territorial Defence of Bihac, the TO there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How long did training last for this second group?

utterances.speaker: SILVIA PALIC-MITRECIC
utterances.text: Training lasted approximately 20 days, 15 to 20 days. These were people who had some war experience, previous war experience.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What about their instructors? Who were the instructors?

utterances.speaker: SILVIA PALIC-MITRECIC
utterances.text: They were members of the Croatian army.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you tell us the locations where the -- the localities where training took place?

utterances.speaker: SILVIA PALIC-MITRECIC
utterances.text: It took place in Boronjaj, that is a barracks belonging to the Croatian army. It is in Zagreb. Zutica in the vicinity of Zagreb, it is a wood where there was a smaller barracks. Zazine was next, on the road towards Sisak, Jastrebarsko and Zdencina. Those were the localities.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What about equipment? How did you -- what about equipment, supplies and quartermaster supplies?

utterances.speaker: SILVIA PALIC-MITRECIC
utterances.text: The military part, that is to say weapons, were organised in such a way that the Croatian army, from its barracks, would give me the weapons, hand them over to me, and I would equip these people, whereas the quartermaster supplies were obtained from abroad, by people from abroad, people from Bihac and the surroundings of Bihac, who found themselves outside the country when the war broke out.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So this second group of some 200 members, how were they transported to Bihac and when?

utterances.speaker: SILVIA PALIC-MITRECIC
utterances.text: This second group with exactly 242 men, started out on the 26th of July. There were 11 buses and 2 trucks. They went to Ogulin, and later on they were taken over by the scouts of Ogulin, that is to say, members of the Slunja regiment, scouts of the Slunja regiment, and they were transported to Bihac.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Ogulin was free territory in Croatia under the command of the Croatian army?

utterances.speaker: SILVIA PALIC-MITRECIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you tell the Court whether a third group was formed ultimately?

utterances.speaker: SILVIA PALIC-MITRECIC
utterances.text: Yes. And there was some interesting things that happened to this third group. In Zagreb a club, local club called Una was set up, a national club, which tried to do something on their own initiative. They tried to do similar work to my own. They would rally anybody who was willing to go to Bihac, and the age span of these individuals was from 18 to 65 years of age. They came to ask me, because they had problems with their lodgings, they wanted me to put them up, and there were 400 people approximately. So with the help of the Zagreb command district, they were put up in Zdencina, that is to say, the environs of Zagreb, where they tried to organise their life and training there. They did not find this very easy, and at the same time, at that same period, another group of young people came to me, they were members of the 101st Brigade of the Croatian army which was located in Posavina, which had been released from the Croatian army with the desire to be transferred to Bihac.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you will tell us, before we move on, the first group that was collected by the club that was called Una and the other group that had left the Croatian army, were they all Muslims as well?

utterances.speaker: SILVIA PALIC-MITRECIC
utterances.text: In 99 per cent of the cases, yes, they were.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What happened next with this third group?

utterances.speaker: SILVIA PALIC-MITRECIC
utterances.text: The third group tried to establish itself in a military fashion, but this proved impossible because of the average age of individuals from Zdencina, and so we tried to organise their transfer to Bihac, which was done successfully, but this first group was a large group, and unfortunately, it did not manage to cross.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Before we go on to say how this happened, tell us, were they trained by instructors of the Croatian army, and did they get the weapons and other equipment from the Croatian army?

utterances.speaker: SILVIA PALIC-MITRECIC
utterances.text: Yes, because there were no other possibilities to this.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When did this group start out across occupied enemy territory?

utterances.speaker: SILVIA PALIC-MITRECIC
utterances.text: On the 25th of August, 1992.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How were they killed?

utterances.speaker: SILVIA PALIC-MITRECIC
utterances.text: Because of the second group, which was able to cross this enemy territory without a single bullet being shot, the Serbs organised traps and minefields, ambushes; and they encountered these minefields, there was fighting, and unfortunately the group was wiped out.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was it true that there were eleven dead and 54 taken prisoner?

utterances.speaker: SILVIA PALIC-MITRECIC
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And they, then, the others went and became members of the BH army; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SILVIA PALIC-MITRECIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: May we have the lights dimmed now, please, because we have two videotapes, amateur videotapes to show you. And while we're looking at the videotapes, could you describe what is happening on them and where the pictures were taken. (Videotape played).

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you describe where this tape was made, if you recognise it?

utterances.speaker: SILVIA PALIC-MITRECIC
utterances.text: This group is in Zdencina. These are people who were formed, a group formed by the local club, Una.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So this is what you were just talking about?

utterances.speaker: SILVIA PALIC-MITRECIC
utterances.text: Yes, and this group did not survive.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: While crossing?

utterances.speaker: SILVIA PALIC-MITRECIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: While the tape is running, and before we move to the tape of another group, could you please tell me whether or not at that time in 1992 you had cooperation with Fikret Abdic?

utterances.speaker: SILVIA PALIC-MITRECIC
utterances.text: Fikret Abdic, at his invitation from Rijeka, because that's where he was staying, I arrived there and we tried to agree on him also forming a group which would be sent to Velika Kladusa. Because of the volume of my work I could not accept that, and by force he imposed a group on me which he sent to me on November 15th. I did not work personally with that group, but I did accept it on the border between Slovenia and Croatia, because that group was formed in Slovenia. That is where it was trained, that is where it was armed, and it was my business to accept the group, receive the group and possibly send them to Bihac.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: These were Muslims?

utterances.speaker: SILVIA PALIC-MITRECIC
utterances.text: Yes, these were all Muslims, these were people who worked in Slovenia and wanted to go back to their places of residence.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you tell us in two or three sentences, who was Fikret Abdic at that time?

utterances.speaker: SILVIA PALIC-MITRECIC
utterances.text: Fikret Abdic was the elected president of Bosnia and Herzegovina, and also member of the presidency of Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did Fikret Abdic tell you where this group was supposed to go?

utterances.speaker: SILVIA PALIC-MITRECIC
utterances.text: Well, no, not exactly.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did anybody arrive from that group to Bihac?

utterances.speaker: SILVIA PALIC-MITRECIC
utterances.text: Because the big group in August did not make it, I did not dare to transfer this other group because I had information there were ambushes and more minefields; so, because of the safety of those people this group was not, this group was disbanded. The weapons were given to me and the weapons were transferred to a port warehouse. The warehouse belonged to the army of Bosnia and Herzegovina, Bihac Territorial Defence.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In Zagreb?

utterances.speaker: SILVIA PALIC-MITRECIC
utterances.text: Yes, in Zagreb.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was it true that 21 men went to Bihac anyway?

utterances.speaker: SILVIA PALIC-MITRECIC
utterances.text: Yes, they went there without my knowledge on their own initiative, and they arrived there, I heard they did get there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Are you familiar that in 1993 two groups, mainly of future officers of Bosnia and Herzegovina, were formed and they were transferred to Bosnia and Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: SILVIA PALIC-MITRECIC
utterances.text: Yes, these people reported to me with the request, not with the desire, but with the request that they wanted to be transferred to Bihac, which is what I did.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did these people leave the Croatian army?

utterances.speaker: SILVIA PALIC-MITRECIC
utterances.text: Yes, they had all been members of the Croatian army, and upon arrival to Bihac they took over command duties, as far as I heard.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is it true that the first group went in March 1993 and the second group in May of 1993?

utterances.speaker: SILVIA PALIC-MITRECIC
utterances.text: Yes, this is true.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: After that you stopped forming groups which were being transferred to Bihac. What was the reason to that?

utterances.speaker: SILVIA PALIC-MITRECIC
utterances.text: This was because the commander of the Territorial Defence, or the army of BH of the 5th Corps from Bihac, said that these people, upon arrival to Bihac, were going to their homes, they were hiding their weapons and were defending their villages, meaning that they were not participating, not all of them, but some of them were not participating in the general defence.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So, the letter, what did it say? Was there a problem with manpower or logistics?

utterances.speaker: SILVIA PALIC-MITRECIC
utterances.text: The problem was in logistics. Personnel was not a problem.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: After that did you start cooperating with the logistics groups of the army of BH who were in Croatia?

utterances.speaker: SILVIA PALIC-MITRECIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Are you familiar with a senior officer of the JNA, his name is Mustafa Porobic, he is a Muslim, former JNA officer, and he formed a military unit from Rijeka which he sent to Bosnia and Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: SILVIA PALIC-MITRECIC
utterances.text: Yes, I know Mr. Porobic, he called me on the telephone, asked me whether it would be, saying would it be good to us to meet so I could help him in his work because of the experience I had. But I had to refuse that because I had other obligations.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know anything about Fikret Cuskic, that he wanted to leave the Croatian army to go to Travnik, Central Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: SILVIA PALIC-MITRECIC
utterances.text: Yes, I know Fikret Cuskic personally, we had contact two or three times. He personally requested to me to transfer him to Bihac. I could not do that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: While he was a commander in Travnik, do you know that his family was in Croatia the whole time?

utterances.speaker: SILVIA PALIC-MITRECIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If we wanted to summarise this information, this data, could you tell us, how many people in total did you help to go to Bosnia and Herzegovina and join the ranks of the Bosnia and Herzegovina army? How many weapons? What are the figures?

utterances.speaker: SILVIA PALIC-MITRECIC
utterances.text: There were 1.240 people. And as far as weapons and equipment, I can read that, may I read my notes?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes, go ahead.

utterances.speaker: SILVIA PALIC-MITRECIC
utterances.text: Sniper rifles, M-74, there were 34. Automatic rifle -- I don't want this to be confusing, because some people were taking two or three rifles. Makarov guns, 32 pieces; automatic Scorpion guns, 19 pieces; submachine guns, 50 pieces; submachine guns M-72, 38 pieces; Zolja hand launched launchers, 47 pieces; hand grenades, 3.484 pieces; semi-automatic rifles, 7 pieces; M-48 rifles, 3 pieces; compasses 107 pieces; 76-milimetre bullets, 600.000 pieces; 7-9 bullets, 300.000.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So, this is what these soldiers of the army of Bosnia and Herzegovina took with them when they went to Bosnia and Herzegovina. You mentioned your group, then later you mentioned Mustafa Porobic's group, who was sending Muslim soldiers from Croatia to Bosnia and Herzegovina; is there a third group that did the same?

utterances.speaker: SILVIA PALIC-MITRECIC
utterances.text: Yes. There was a group of people from Mesihat.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is that the Islamic religious community in Croatia?

utterances.speaker: SILVIA PALIC-MITRECIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's right, which organised in the mosque in Zagreb, it organised groups of people and sent them to Travnik.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Could we see another film, please, another tape? (Videotape played)

utterances.speaker: SILVIA PALIC-MITRECIC
utterances.text: This is still in Zdencina, the same big group of people which was organised by the local club, Una.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: They are now leaving?

utterances.speaker: SILVIA PALIC-MITRECIC
utterances.text: Yes, they are leaving. This is shortly -- this is about ten days before they set out.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Zdencina, how far is that in relation to Zagreb?

utterances.speaker: SILVIA PALIC-MITRECIC
utterances.text: It's about 18 kilometres from Zagreb, towards Karlovac.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. We will not watch this until the end.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Mr. President, we have finished our direct examination, and we submit this tape as Defence Exhibit.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: No objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: No objections? All right it, will be admitted.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: This is D490A to the first part that was shown, and B to the part we have just seen.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Mr. Kehoe?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President, thank you. Cross-examined by Mr. Kehoe.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Good morning Mrs. Palic-Mitrecic. My name is Greg Kehoe and my colleague Mark Harmon is beside me to my right, welcome. You mentioned at the end of your testimony that you assisted 1.240 soldiers, a series of arms. This was going into the Bihac pocket; wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: SILVIA PALIC-MITRECIC
utterances.text: That's right, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And all you've told us about was going into the Bihac pocket, your assistance; was it not?

utterances.speaker: SILVIA PALIC-MITRECIC
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you mentioned just lastly this mosque was gathering people to send them to Travnik. When in 1992 was that?

utterances.speaker: SILVIA PALIC-MITRECIC
utterances.text: I can't tell you the exact date to the simple reason that I had a lot of other work to do. But I do know that they did this.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was it when you were --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Mr. Nobilo, do you have an objection?

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: In fact, yes, the way in which the answer, the question was posed. He said "when was that," and then he said the Prosecutor said "1992," which the witness never mentioned. So, this is an attempt to lead the witness, because she does not know when they sent the group.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: But the witness should be able to answer this kind of question, to overcome that kind of a problem. But anyway, Mr. Kehoe, ask your question a different way, please.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Ma'am, did this take place when you were assisting the rest of these people to go to Bihac in 1992? Is that when the mosque was getting these people to go to Travnik? Was it during that same time frame?

utterances.speaker: SILVIA PALIC-MITRECIC
utterances.text: Both during 1992, the second half of 1992 and in 1993.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. When in 1993 was this mosque bringing people together to go to Travnik?

utterances.speaker: SILVIA PALIC-MITRECIC
utterances.text: I can't give you an answer to that to the simple reason that I had other assignments to work on. But I know that the mosque did this, but I did not participate in it directly, so I can't actually tell you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And who was it in this mosque that was gathering these troops to send them to Travnik in 1992 and 1993?

utterances.speaker: SILVIA PALIC-MITRECIC
utterances.text: They were all stories, rumours, but I don't know the individuals myself, so I don't know the names, either.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So, it would be accurate to say that this was a story that you heard and you don't have any first-hand knowledge about it?

utterances.speaker: SILVIA PALIC-MITRECIC
utterances.text: Not first-hand knowledge, no, because I didn't work with them, as I said.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So, is that the reason why you don't exactly know when these troops were going to the Travnik area?

utterances.speaker: SILVIA PALIC-MITRECIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, lastly, you mentioned Fikret Abdic. And Fikret Abdic, I believe sometime in the fall, well maybe the winter, I think you said November of 1992, Fikret Abdic came to you to train some troops; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SILVIA PALIC-MITRECIC
utterances.text: In August.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm sorry, maybe I misheard you. August of 1992. Now, this was before he had broken with the Sarajevo government, and this was before he had joined with the army of the Republic of Serb Krajina; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: SILVIA PALIC-MITRECIC
utterances.text: I can't answer that, because it was not one of the things I thought about.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you, Ma'am. I don't think I have any other questions, let me just talk to my colleague to one moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Mr. President, Judge Shahabuddeen, no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Judge Shahabuddeen?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Madam, would you confirm my impression that the second clip which we saw bore the date of August 1992?

utterances.speaker: SILVIA PALIC-MITRECIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Thank you, madam. That's all we need you to do. The Tribunal would like to express its gratitude to you for having come to The Hague, and now send you back to the responsibilities as the head of your private company. Very well, thank you very much. This is a long afternoon, so we might take a short break now if there is no problem with that, Mr. Registrar? All right, we're going to take a 10-minute break. Let the Judges leave the courtroom and then someone will take care of you, madam. We will resume in about ten minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: We can now resume the hearing. All right. Mr. Hayman, I just wanted to say that by Friday, at the end of our hearing, the registrar will tell us how much time you have left, how many witnesses we've heard and we'll try to evaluate how things stand for January, all right? Is it possible? But of course, the list that you have will remain confidential. Thank you. We can move to the next witness now. Mr. Nobilo or Mr. Hayman?

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Mr. President, Dusko Lukovic, or Dusan Lukovic will be our next witness. (The witness entered court)

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Do you hear me, Mr. Lukovic? You are at the International Criminal Tribunal. Please tell us your name, your given age, your given name, your age, your residence, and then remain standing for a few more moments, as long as it takes to read the oath. Please go ahead.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I am Dusan Lukovic. My father was Bosko. Born on 22nd of September, 1935 in Banja Luka, Bosnia-Herzegovina. I am a Serb by nationality, an atheist. By vocation I am a sociology professor and I have been living in Vitez for a full 40 years, since 1958. I am retired, I have -- I became a pensioner on the 1st of May, 1996.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Please take the oath.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Thank you. You are at the International Tribunal. You've been called by the Defence. You can be seated. You have been called by the accused's counsel, who is in this Tribunal. We thank you for coming. First you're going to be asked some questions by the Defence counsel, then by the Office of the Prosecutor, and possibly the Judges may have a few questions to ask you as well. Proceed, please, Mr. Nobilo.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Examined by Mr. Nobilo:

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Lukovic, let us repeat: You were born in 1935, were you not?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN LUKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You are a Serb by nationality and an atheist with regard to religion. Can you explain to the Court up until the war, that is to say, the war in Bosnia-Herzegovina in 1992, what duties did you perform? What was your work in Vitez and other places as well perhaps? Explain it to the Trial Chamber, please.

utterances.speaker: DUSAN LUKOVIC
utterances.text: I performed several important duties, and I'm going to enumerate the more numerous ones. I was director of the Workers' University.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Would you explain what Workers' University is and where it was located?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN LUKOVIC
utterances.text: The Workers' University was located in Vitez, in the cultural centre there. It is educational institution for adults. It engaged in cultural activities and various forms of professional training for workers. Then I was the director of a secondary school centre in Vitez, and one of the directors of the military factories, Slobodan Princip Selo, and in the interim periods from 1976 to 1980 I was the Vice-President of the municipal assembly of Vitez, or as you would say, deputy mayor, as you would say today. In 1983 and 1984 I was president of the municipal assembly. That was the first mandate, and the second mandate was in 1984/1985, once between president of the municipal assembly.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Of Vitez you mean?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN LUKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, of Vitez. In 1984 I was president of the community of the municipality of Travnik, Novi Travnik and Vitez, and as I said at the beginning, I have been living in Vitez for 41 years now. This is my 41st year and I know the conditions prevailing in Vitez very well. So much in answer to your question.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: May I ask you to make breaks between the questions and answers? In 1993, when the war conflicts broke out in the Vitez municipality, how old were you?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN LUKOVIC
utterances.text: I was -- I was born in 1935, which makes me 58 years old at the time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you ever in the combat units of the Croatian Defence Council? Were you involved in that?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN LUKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I was member of a work platoon.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what about the combat units?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN LUKOVIC
utterances.text: No, I was not, because I was over 55 years of age and I -- my military duties went up to the age of 60.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tell us what you know about the work platoons. You said you were engaged in a work platoon. Can you tell us when this began, what tasks you were assigned, who organised the work platoons and what kind of jobs you did? Would you explain this to the Trial Chamber, please?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN LUKOVIC
utterances.text: I am one of the participants of a work platoon, and so my testimony will go along the lines of what you've just asked me. Work platoons in Vitez were organised by the defence department of Vitez and the Civil Defence service.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You can, of course, use your notes, but please try and speak a little more slowly, please, and make pauses. You mentioned the Civil Defence and the defence department. Can you tell the Court whether this represents civilian organs in Vitez power and authority?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN LUKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, these were civilian organs. And while civil protection had work, they had work platoons --

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Excuse me, Mr. President. I'm going to object to the witness reading from notes unless he needs those notes to refresh his recollection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Do you need your notes in order to refresh your memory, Mr. Lukovic, or is this a declaration or a statement which you've already prepared?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN LUKOVIC
utterances.text: I'm going to use them very briefly, just to systematise what I want to say.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: The Tribunal would appreciate your answering questions from memory. You carried out your responsibilities for 40 years, therefore, you must be very familiar with that subject. You can consult documents for notes or figures, for example, which you may not have in your mind, but it is not proper for you to read a statement because it would distort the proceedings. In most legal systems, that is civil law or common-law, the witness testifies, and if he bases his comments on documents, which have to be provided to the opposing party, or asks for authorisation for documents in order to refresh his memory, which is normal, and if you so wish, we will authorise you to do so, but if you don't mind, please answer spontaneously when the questions are asked. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: DUSAN LUKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I can and I apologise. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: No, no no, you don't have to apologise.

utterances.speaker: DUSAN LUKOVIC
utterances.text: So the work platoons, the work platoons that were established by the department for defence had, as their task, to assist the armed component in the field to perform trench digging, communicating trenches, dugouts and to prepare the terrain for defence, in fact, the defence of those units, so that the frontline could be defended and so as to ensure as little human casualties as possible.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tell me, you were involved in the work platoons. When were you asked to join a work platoon for the first time?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN LUKOVIC
utterances.text: In June, 1993.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you were called up, was this a uni-national platoon or multi-ethnic?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN LUKOVIC
utterances.text: I travelled around several places, but they were all multi-ethnic work platoons. They were not only made up of the Croats, or Serbs or Muslims, but the ones that I participated in we had both Croats, and Serbs and Muslims, and there were some Romanies as well.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you explain to the Court how you came to make up one of these work platoons? Who invited you to join them and who told you that you would go trench digging?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN LUKOVIC
utterances.text: One day the Military Police came to my front door and they asked, "Lukovic, Dusan?" I identified myself, and they told me to report urgently to the city library, which is where I went, and they told me that I was mobilised into a work platoon and they said that we should go to our assignment.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tell the Court, please, how did you understand this, that it was on a voluntary basis, that it was compulsory? What did you think?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN LUKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, I knew the regulations fairly well, and I knew my duties as a military recruit, so that I accepted this as a military duty, and I considered that mobilisation, this act was an act where I, as a citizen, would have to respond to the act. If I did not, sanctions would be applied. So I accepted this as my duty, as the duty of each and every citizen who has not reached the age of 60.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you explain to the Court the locations you went to? First of all, let us enumerate the places where you did this trench digging.

utterances.speaker: DUSAN LUKOVIC
utterances.text: I said a moment ago I went to Zvijezda, that is a locality where there is a mountain centre, mountaineering centre, and then Zaselje, which is a little lower down from Zvijezda, which is at a higher altitude. Then we have Bobasi. That was the borderline toward Kruscica. Then Brdjani. That is also in the vicinity of Bobasi. Lazine, which is by the village of Tolovici. Barin Gaj, that is near the village of Ahmici. After that part, our work platoon was used for omni purposes. In November 1993 I was once again called up for mobilisation by the Civil Defence department was engaged once again in the general purpose units.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Thank you. We're now going to hand out a photocopy of two documents that you gave me, so may we have it placed on the -- they are two ID's, and we'll try and read it out with the help of our interpreters. We have two documents. First of all, the individual, that is to say, the first page of the ID card and the reverse side of it.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: This number -- this document is 491.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Could you please have copies given to the interpreters? I think there is a sufficient number of copies. May we have the ELMO switched on, please, and have it enlarged, a close-up of the document, please? The second document, the second paper. It comes first. Yes, another paper. Okay.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm going to read the text. It is: The Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina. That is on the left-hand side. The Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna. The Croatian Defence Council. Identification: Dusan. The father's name Bosko. Surname Lukovic. Born in 1935. And the ID number is 824. It is the department for defence of Vitez, that is the stamp. On the right-hand side the same identification, except that it says "Dusko" instead of "Dusan ." All the other elements are the same. On the reverse side, on the left-hand side we have -- it is the civil ID, which is a public document, which proves membership in the Vitez municipality and its defence, and it says Civil Defence and work platoon, the name it had was Kolonija. Below that it says a member, and it is signed by the authorised individuals. The date is the 14th of January, 1994, whereas on the right-hand side we have the same text. It is once again that the ID is a public document which shows that it was issued by the Vitez department, and it says work platoon-Kolonija. It says member once again, and the date is the 20th of July, 1993. Tell us, please, is this your ID as a member of the work platoon?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN LUKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, it is, but it lacks a photograph which I have used, but I do have the original, which I have brought with me. It was used if we were to return from the terrain. This would be an ID for us we encountered any checkpoints or controls.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tell us, the work platoon named Kolonija, that is the name of your particular unit? What was it named after?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN LUKOVIC
utterances.text: The town of Vitez is small, and as there was a military factory there which built these houses for their workers to reside in, it was called the Kolonija, so this is a name that dates back to 1957 when the Kolonija buildings were built.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So, in fact, it is an area of Vitez, a district of Vitez.

utterances.speaker: DUSAN LUKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tell the Court, please, what the working conditions were like on the frontlines. What did it look like in practical terms?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN LUKOVIC
utterances.text: Those of us who were members of a work platoon, whenever we came to the locality where we did our work we would be transported either by a Kombi van or a small bus, especially when we went to Bobasi, Zaselje, Zabrdje and even up to Tolovici, and when there was no fighting going on. Furthermore, when we were on location we were supplied with food, we were given food, and we had three meals, we were given three meals. Most frequently, we would take our meals with the members of the HVO, the armed component of the HVO. If we stayed for one day and then went back at night, we would usually stay one day, but sometimes we would stay three or five days, and then we were put up. We were ensured rest, we were able to sleep. Of course, these were not comfortable houses, they were weekend cottages that had been slightly destroyed, or a house that could be used for that purpose, but the main thing was that we were put up there and we could have a rest and sleep. Furthermore, the terrain where we did our work was secured, and the members of the HVO endeavoured to make it a secure area. They introduced us to the terrain and told us of the positions of the other side, the hostile side to the HVO, where you could die from being hit by a sniper or some other weapon, and they explained to us how we should move about to avoid being hit by the enemy. We were given our tasks and the commander of the frontline would always tell us what we were expected to do, what kind of work. And the essential thing is, in addition to what I already said, was that we were not forced to work beyond endurance. Although, we had to dig with various tools that we had, it often rained, we had picks and axes and shovels and so on. Therefore, I think that the danger at these frontlines, there was a danger at some places, like Bobasi, and then we would stop working; but in other localities this danger did not exist so we were able to perform our work.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tell us, did you gain the impression that the members of the HVO, the soldiers, were correct in their conduct to you; or didn't they care less what happened to you?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN LUKOVIC
utterances.text: As I said, when we were brought on the spot the commander of the frontline would take us over, so he was the commanding officer of all the HVO members, as well, and would assign tasks to us. He would also give us some soldiers to watch over us, and they ensured our safety and security so that nothing would happen. I have several examples. We dug trenches at Zabrdje, and one day we were digging, and we continued the following day and around about noon we were told to interrupt our work and to withdraw urgently and that we would be going back home because they received reports that members of the BH army were preparing a surprise attack on Zabrdje. And then they engaged four soldiers, I think four, perhaps five, with automatic rifles who escorted us to a place of safety, to Zazine. A similar case occurred when we went trench digging during the night and dugouts in Bobasi, and in the morning there was an attack by the BH army and we withdrew on that occasion from that locality to a weekend cottage area and we were allowed to go home. Or another example which took place in Tolovici or Lazine where we were engaged in expanding the trenches and communicating trenches and dugouts. But as this was very close to the BH army positions, they told us that we would have to get up earlier and work until there was, until the mist and fog lasted, because this prevented them from seeing us and shooting at us from snipers. As soon as the mist lifted we would interrupt our work and be taken to places of safety. While we were working, members of the HVO who had time on their hands because there was no fighting actually on the frontline, they, too, would take up the picks and shovels and help us dig the trenches.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Would you please speak more slowly for the sake of the interpreters? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you please tell the Court whether you noticed any inequality in treatment in terms of the members of different ethnic groups? Was one ethnic group sent to more dangerous positions and the other part of the work platoon that belonged to different ethnic groups, were they spared? Did you notice that kind of treatment?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN LUKOVIC
utterances.text: No. That was not the kind of treatment that was accorded to all of us. They tried to protect all of us. We tried to do our work as quickly as possible so that we could be off afterwards and then we could go back. I worked with the Muslims the most, and I did not notice any insults or any mistreatment or any difference, really. I don't know, perhaps I was older than others and therefore more responsible, but it seemed to me that I worked harder than the younger people. It was a strenuous job, but it wasn't exhausting altogether, and we took breaks, so there was no discrimination.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Please tell the Court, was it dangerous, nevertheless, to dig these trenches? What was the danger involved? You have described some of this already, but did you feel safer in Vitez or at the frontline?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN LUKOVIC
utterances.text: When you say frontline, it means danger. But when speaking of Vitez and the fighting that took place in Vitez, it is very difficult to define what the frontline actually is. It is true that the frontline was the first line that divided the two sides. I must say that in Bobasi when the attack took place, we withdrew quickly, and I think that only one person was wounded, although there was over a hundred of us, there were even more Croats than others in Bobasi. At the other places it was not dangerous. I'm even prepared to claim that it was more dangerous for me to be in Vitez when I was off, when I didn't go to work, because Vitez was shelled very often by mortars and tank grenades. For example, I lived in a three-room apartment, and two of my grandsons were injured when a shrapnel got into the bedroom where my wife was, too, and all the glass on the windows broke. And this also happened in the villages, in Vitez even, eight children were killed by shells and grenades, and a child was killed in his father's hands, in his father's arms. So, to be fair, it was even safer at the frontline, but it was more difficult. There was more hardship involved, that's what I'm trying to say, but it was better. In town and in the villages it was considerably more difficult, only if the fighting actually broke out, then; but then there were no civilians around.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tell me, in terms of status, how did you regulate this? You did contribute in a way to the defence of Vitez, not with a rifle in your hands, but you worked and you fortified the necessary facilities; so, how was your status regulated in terms of participation in the defence of Vitez?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN LUKOVIC
utterances.text: All of us who took part in the work platoons, I'm talking about work platoons, and the same goes for the members of the HVO, all of those who were engaged in combat and in work platoons, these are counted as years of service. So, if you were at frontline either as a member of the work platoon or in a combat unit, your years of service were doubled, and since I was a pensioner already, this became part of my pension, as well. Also recently we received documents where part of our military pay, as it is called, was given to us, actually all of us who were in the work platoons and those who were in the armed units. When I say all, I'm saying that the Serbs, the Romanies, the Muslims, the Croats, all of those who participated got equal shares.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So, can we conclude that your participation in the war with a shovel in your hands, in terms of status, in terms of your retirement entitlement and years of service et cetera, has been made equal to that of an HVO who fought with a rifle in his hands?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN LUKOVIC
utterances.text: (No audible response).

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you please repeat your answer into the microphone?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN LUKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, it was quite equal.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: That will be all, Mr. President, as far as the examination-in-chief is concerned. We would like to offer these IDs, D491, as a Defence exhibit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: (Interpreter's microphone not on).

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. President, Judge Shahabuddeen, good afternoon, Counsel. Cross-examined by Mr. Harmon:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. Lukovic, my name is Mark Harmon, I'm one of the Prosecutors in this case, and sitting to my right is Mr. Gregory Kehoe, welcome to The Hague. Mr. Lukovic, I'm reviewing my notes and your testimony; you indicated that the work platoon, which you became a member, started in June of 1993; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN LUKOVIC
utterances.text: Perhaps you didn't understand me. I came to participate in the work platoon only in June, 1993. Until then I was not engaged by anyone, I was in the records listed as a reservist. But the work platoons were established somewhat earlier, as soon as the fighting started the work platoons were established.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When were the work platoons established, and how were they established? Were they established by legislation?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN LUKOVIC
utterances.text: I cannot give you the exact date when they were established, because I was asked to join in June. But as far as I managed to find out later, they were established as soon as the fighting broke out between the HVO and the members of the army of Bosnia and Herzegovina. This subject matter was regulated in the law on national defence earlier on, before. None of this was new, the civilian defence has work platoons and the military component has work platoons. Now, I accepted this as my duty and my obligation, and in Vitez during the period of the political government of the HVO this was regulated by a decree, a decree on the armed forces of the Croat community of Herceg-Bosna. So with your permission I could read out a few details.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Lukovic, let me ask you some questions and I will come to that decree perhaps later in my examination. Mr. Lukovic, in April of 1993, were you aware that a number of Muslim civilians were detained at the Dubravica elementary school?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN LUKOVIC
utterances.text: The colleagues that I had, a professor of sociology and other friends of mine, were detained at the adult education centre. I worked in Vitez, so I can't really tell you about Dubravica or other facilities. They told me when the fighting broke out and the shelling started that there was a certain division in this group, and I cannot really assert anything as far as Dubravica is concerned, and I don't want to give you half truths; but I did hear that in Dubravica a number of Muslims from that area were kept there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And were you, you told us you were informed that a number of Muslims were detained at the Vitez cinema complex; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN LUKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you informed that Muslims were also detained at the Vitez veterinary station?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN LUKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I heard about the veterinary station too.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you informed that the HVO detained Muslims civilians in the SDK offices in Vitez?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN LUKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you informed that the HVO detained Muslim civilians in a few houses in the village of Gacice?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN LUKOVIC
utterances.text: I didn't hear that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you informed that the HVO detained Muslim civilians in the Kiseljak barracks?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN LUKOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you informed that the HVO detained Muslim civilians at the municipal building in Kiseljak?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN LUKOVIC
utterances.text: No, no. I can really speak of Vitez only, but I'm sorry, when I said that I heard of these other things, I heard about all of that from my friends. I heard about Dubravica, the SDK, and also a colleague of mine who was at the adult education centre told me about this. I was director of that establishment before and he told me they were kept in the cinema of that centre.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Lastly, and tell me if you know this, were you informed that the HVO detained Muslim civilians a the Kaonik prison?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN LUKOVIC
utterances.text: I heard about Kaonik. I also have some friends who were in HVO units who were also sent to prison in Kaonik, and they spent 10 to 15 days there, because they had committed certain misdemeanours at the frontlines. So, that is how I came to the conclusion that this was a prison, both for members of the HVO who violated military rules.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Lukovic, were you aware that the HVO forced those Muslim prisoners who were detained at those locations which I have identified to go to frontline positions where combat activities were taking place and forced them to dig trenches?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN LUKOVIC
utterances.text: No, no, I have not been informed of that, so I cannot confirm that for you. I mean, I was there where there was shooting, but no one would dig where there was shooting. And you know, I'm a Serb and I stayed there, and perhaps some of the Muslims stayed with the Croats, and then perhaps somebody could have a different view of all of this. But I consider this to be my obligation, and perhaps some of these Muslims who were digging out there together with me, one of them was the president of the municipal assembly before that, another one was a colleague of mine, a teacher, and another one was a musician, and also there was a Muslim who was sleeping indoors on a sofa, and perhaps my story is different and perhaps his story is different. Because as soon as he got an opportunity he left HVO controlled territory, it is only natural, he joined his own people. I'm sorry made this digression.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Please answer the Judges. When you answer, would you look at Judges, please?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Lukovic, it's all right to look at me when I ask the questions, but when you give your response would you please look toward the Judges in giving your responses? Were you aware, Mr. Lukovic, that on April 16th of 1993, and through a considerable period thereafter, that Muslim civilians who were detained at those locations were forcibly kept at frontline positions and forced to dig trenches in exceedingly dangerous conditions?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN LUKOVIC
utterances.text: You know what? I'm talking about work platoons, but I shall answer your question. All of those who were at the adult education centre, none of them went out to dig trenches while they were detained in that building. This was a moment when an all out attack was launched, and the shelling of Vitez, and shooting, et cetera, et cetera; and in that kind of a situation the military authorities probably know why they did that, because children and women were not engaged, only military aged men. I assume that this is done in other situations, too, and it is very hard to define what kind of a war this was. Until only the other day we were colleagues and friends and we lived together and then the shooting started, and then there was a dilemma; where people would go and what side they would take. I dare not claim this, but perhaps the fact that some of the Muslims were kept in a certain place prevented irresponsible individuals from committing a crime.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Lukovic, your testimony was, and I am quoting it, that "None of them," referring to the Muslims at the cinema building, "went out to dig trenches while they were detained in that building." Did you go to the Vitez cinema building between the time period of April the 15th to, say, the second week in May?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN LUKOVIC
utterances.text: To be quite honest, when the fighting began I stayed with my grandchildren and my wife and my daughter-in-law and tried to save my life, to tell you the truth. My son was already at the frontline, and he fought with weapons. So I didn't go there, and to be quite frank, it didn't even cross my mind to leave the apartment. You don't know what it was like for us elderly people who were civilians out there. Later, and later, I was told by the people who were there who worked with me in the factory or wherever, that they were treated fairly, that they were not mistreated, that they were grouped, that is a fact, but they were staying in that building.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So, not having been to the Vitez cinema, and I take it not having been to the frontlines where active combat was taking place, you don't know whether or not those people who were detained in the Vitez cinema building were forcibly taken out against their will to go dig trenches; do you?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN LUKOVIC
utterances.text: Everything I told you about the cinema and about all these other places is hearsay. That is what my Muslim colleagues and friends told me. Those who were there. None of them told me they went out to dig trenches. And afterwards, after a certain period of time when they were returned to their homes, those who remained in Vitez and did not leave Vitez, some went to Travnik, Zenica, and Croats came from Jajce, et cetera, and from Zenica. This was a migration, simply. A large migration, at that. So, whoever remained probably had to join the work platoon because they were military aged men and they had, and they were citizens of Vitez. I'm not a Croat, either, and they were Muslims. But we had to carry out our work duty, and that is the way I understood it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Lukovic, between April 16th, 1993 and the second week of May, 1993, do you know how many Muslim civilians were wounded or killed at the frontline while they were being forced to dig trenches by the HVO?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN LUKOVIC
utterances.text: I don't know. I really don't know. I told you that I knew about my friend Galijasevic, who was wounded in Bobasi, and I know that a Croat was killed in Barin Gaj by Ahmici. So there were killings and woundings on all sides, not only Serbs and Muslims, my son was also wounded at the frontline. I don't know. I really don't know. And what I do know, I told about that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let me just stay with that point for just a minute, Mr. Lukovic. You described the conditions that you experienced as a member of a work platoon from the time of June of 1993 onwards. Do you know about the conditions that the Muslim civilians that were forced to dig trenches experienced between April 16, 1993 and, say, the second week of May 1993?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN LUKOVIC
utterances.text: I don't. I don't know. I only told you about the places where I was and where I can make assertions, and tell the truth and tell you about what it was like where I was.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, let me -- could I have the assistance of the usher in getting the easel? I'm going to put a map up on the easel, and I'm going to ask you to please, with a coloured pen, please mark the locations where you, as the member of a work platoon went to dig trenches, but while that's being set up let me ask you some additional questions. When you say that in June of 1993, the Military Police came to your residence and advised you to report to a particular location, in other words, you were mobilised, you said that you believed that you had a duty and a responsibility to fulfil whatever obligations existed upon you. Do you remember that testimony?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN LUKOVIC
utterances.text: I didn't say whatever obligations. I was told that I should urgently report at the city library, and I found people who work in the civilian defence, I found them there, and they know me. They said to me, "Dusan Lukovic, you have been mobilised and you are a member of the work platoon Kolonija."

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, after you were informed that you were a member of the work platoon Kolonija, did you stay with that particular work platoon and perform the duties that you've described at the frontlines exclusively with that work platoon Kolonija or did you work with other work platoons?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN LUKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, yes, Kolonija is big, so depending on what was needed on the ground -- I'm sorry. I worked at Zabrdje only for two days, and Zaselje only one day, one day, in Bobasi two days, in Brdjani three days. So it really depended on the necessity involved and on the situation on the ground, on what the situation was like in terms of dugouts, trenches, communication trenches, et cetera. Then only in November 1993, because I was sick for a certain period of time, I caught a cold at Zabrdje, so I had sick leave for about one month. I had an inflammation, and I was under medical control all the time, and a doctor treated me. So that's what I can tell you. But if we are talking about Muslims, Bosniaks, I know them very well. Some of them were my students, just like there were some Croat soldiers who were my students too, et cetera. So for this period, while I was there and in the places where I was, no one was mistreated, really, but you just had to work. Perhaps I didn't elaborate on this, I just talked about transportation, et cetera, but you have to understand the war conditions. In spite of all the high offices I held, I complied with this without any objections. They could have offered me to do something in the civilian defence. I wouldn't have been a commander or whatever, but if they asked me to work I did work. I even understood that if I worked this way, it will help the young people, less young people would get killed. So that is what I had in mind.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Lukovic, beside the work platoon Kolonija were there other work platoons that had other names?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN LUKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Most of these work platoons were called by the place that the people came from. So Donja Veceriska, Nadioci, et cetera. The name of the work platoon coincided with the name of the village. So I live in Kolonija, which is actually a certain part of the town, and that is why my work platoon was called Kolonija.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know the other names of the work platoons beside the platoon Kolonija?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN LUKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, I just told you. Nadioci work platoon, Donja Veceriska work platoon, Stari Bila. I cannot remember right now, but it -- all of these were villages on HVO controlled territory, and that's where the armed forces of the HVO were too.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, let me ask you briefly, what would happen to you, if you know, if you refused to participate in a work platoon? What was the consequence?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN LUKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, as I was describing this decree, I said that it existed, and then there's also a law, and any non-compliance with the law and non-compliance with the military obligation -- everybody, every citizen has military duties, and if they do not fulfil them then this is a misdemeanour. So I would have been taken to a municipal Judge, and perhaps I would have even been taken to prison, depending on how -- on how my offence was judged and whether I should spend time in gaol even.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, will you assist me please, Mr. Lukovic, I'm going to have the usher give you this pen, and you have testified that you went to various locations where you dug trenches. Would you take this pen and please mark those locations where you dug trenches? There is a map.

utterances.speaker: DUSAN LUKOVIC
utterances.text: I don't know how well I'll do on this map, you know, because this is a photocopy. I don't know. I'll do my best, but could somebody please show this to me and--

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: May I assist the witness, Mr. President?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Perhaps Mr. Nobilo would like to approach the map as well.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let me assist you, please. Here is Vitez.

utterances.speaker: DUSAN LUKOVIC
utterances.text: Vitez -- (not audible). Can I underline this? May I underline this? Tolovici, Persinje, Alinja, Bukve, Preocica. Kruscica is down here. Zabrdje is down here. Zabrdje, Zaselje is over here. Zabrdje is somewhere here. Is it possible that Zabrdje isn't on the map? Zvijezda is above Zabrdje. Kruscica, Hrasno Sivrino Selo, Ahmici. I was here in Barin Gaj. Bobasi should be somewhere in this region. Kruscica. It should be somewhere here.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Why don't you put a line in the area where you can best approximate where you dug trenches?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN LUKOVIC
utterances.text: Bobasi, Brdjani.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Put a line where you --

utterances.speaker: DUSAN LUKOVIC
utterances.text: It's from Vitez towards Kruscica, along the boarder. Attacks came from this side. Does that satisfy you?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, let me ask you. You said Bobasi, and is this the line that -- this is Bobasi?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN LUKOVIC
utterances.text: Here, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Where is Lazine?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN LUKOVIC
utterances.text: Lazine, Tolovici. Laizne is Tolovici.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Barin Gaj?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN LUKOVIC
utterances.text: Zasilje, and we remained here at Zabrdje. This was the mountaineering hut. Zabrdje, Zaselje Bobasi, Brdjani, Barin Gaj, Tolovici and Lazine.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Are these marks in orange all the locations where you, as a member of the Kolonija work platoon, went to dig trenches? Let me ask you that question again. Are these the locations in orange -- do these represent all of the locations where you, as a member of the Kolonija work platoon, went to dig trenches?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN LUKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Please have a seat again. Thank you. Thank you for assisting me in that, Mr. Lukovic. Let me ask you, you said, as well, in your experiences at these frontlines, that you went up to these particular locations on a number of occasions. How many times did you go to dig trenches, to the best your recollection, during the time that you were a member of the work platoon?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN LUKOVIC
utterances.text: I can't tell you exactly. I would stay for 15 days at some places, and for three days, for example, we would go home and then be taken back. In Barin Gaj for example, I think I spent 18 days at Barin Gaj. In Zaselje I spent two days. In Brdjani I spent three days. So it wasn't a continuous period that I spent in the work platoons. You would do the work and then go home, and then they would call you up again to the same work platoon or they would add some men to the work platoon. Somebody would be ill and then they would send you somewhere else. But regardless of what they wanted me to do, I went to all these different locations which were under HVO control.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And throughout the period of time you were a member of the work platoon Kolonija, how many people were killed or injured while digging at frontline positions?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN LUKOVIC
utterances.text: I was witness to one killing by sniper fire, and he was a Croat. I think his name was Anto. Whether it was Zeko or Zekic I don't remember exactly. Also, Galijasevic Senad was wounded, my friend, but he was transferred immediately to the war hospital at Nova Bila and was treated there. His life was saved. And there was another, Karadza, had some light injuries, some scratches, Ahmed, and he was also transferred to a medical unit. That is as far as I know, the ones I witnessed in the work platoons myself.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, Senad Galic, what is his ethnic group?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN LUKOVIC
utterances.text: Galijasevic is a Muslim.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Ahmed Karadza who was injured, what was his ethnic group?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN LUKOVIC
utterances.text: Also a Muslim.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How old was Senad Galic? How old was he?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN LUKOVIC
utterances.text: He is Sead. Senad is a musician Zagreb, Senad of Bosnia. This is Sead. He was about 40. I'd also like to mention, if I may, before I was -- Galijasevic was wounded, I was on the spot at exactly the position he was digging, and I went outside the trenches because I had to sign for the number of meals we were given. I could have been the victim on that particular occasion. The sniper could have hit me. But he was digging, he probably stood up and was hit by a sniper. As I say, he was not killed. He was given excellent medical assistance so he's quite well now and there are no consequences of that wound.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, did I understand your testimony, Mr. Lukovic, that one of the people who was in your work platoon was the President of the municipal assembly, or did I misunderstand that portion of your testimony?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN LUKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes, you understood it correctly. He replaced me when my mandate expired. His name was Viteskic Mirsad. I think he resides in Germany now. Before that he was secretary of the Committee of the League of Communists of Bosnia-Herzegovina. He was there with me. There was another musician, Dzevad nicknamed Dzedzo. He was president and we dug together, we dug a trench together.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That was the individual who was the former president of the municipal assembly. Was he a Muslim, a Croat or a Serb?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN LUKOVIC
utterances.text: He was a Muslim.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, you testified that the various groups that were work platoons were integrated, they included Muslims, Serbs, Croats. Were there work platoons that were work platoons consisting of exclusively of Muslims, exclusively of Croats, exclusively of Serbs, if you know?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN LUKOVIC
utterances.text: I'm not aware of that. The work platoons where I was engaged, they were all multi-ethnic in composition.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, in part you testified that at the conclusion of your service in the work platoon -- first of all, when did that end? First of all, can you tell us when you stopped working in the work platoon?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN LUKOVIC
utterances.text: I stopped working in the work platoon -- I'll have to look at my notes. May I do so--

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Please.

utterances.speaker: DUSAN LUKOVIC
utterances.text: -- to refresh my memory. Thank you. It was in Barin Gaj. I was there from the 11th to the 23rd of October, 1993. From November I was transferred to the Civil Defence work platoon, where I worked as a guard and guarded the Red Cross vehicles and other vehicles which were used to bring in the dead and wounded. There was a mortuary there and some building material. I was there from November until April, because I suffered from influenza and I was ill, and I was older, and so they gave me this post in the town of Vitez proper.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
