utterances.text: Now, if a member of a work platoon did not want to go to the frontlines where the enemy was a short distance away, could he refuse to do that?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN LUKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, he could refuse but sanctions would have been applied. He didn't have to go, they wouldn't make him go and use weapons to compel him to go. As I said a moment ago, had I not accepted work in the work platoon, once again the civilian authorities would have written a report and I would have gone before a magistrate and perhaps I would have gotten 7, 10, 15 days in prison as punishment, and they would ask me once again at a later date to perform my duty. But nobody was compelled to do so, that is to say, at gunpoint. Nobody did that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, while you were at these various locations digging trenches, did you see any high ranking members of the HVO military present?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN LUKOVIC
utterances.text: First of all, if you mean a colonel, a general or something of that rank --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you tell us which high ranking members of the HVO were present when you and other members of the work platoon were digging trenches at frontline positions?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN LUKOVIC
utterances.text: Usually they were commanders of the frontline. Whether they were corporals or first lieutenants or something. Azinovic Ilija, for example, was a captain. He had a bigger frontline to command. He enabled us to go to one of these houses, the last house that remained in Ahmici, and we spend the night there. So there were always commanders. Whether they were privates first class or whether slightly higher officers.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Lukovic, did you see any ranking officers of the HVO present at locations where you and other members of the Colonial work platoon were digging trenches?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN LUKOVIC
utterances.text: I said if you think that a -- if you're thinking of a colonel or a major or general, I did not, but I saw captains, those with the rank of captain. He was captain in Barin Gaj and he was there permanently. We go for consultations to Vitez and then return to Barin Gaj, and he would tour the frontlines, as would the others. But they were commanders of 10 or 30 men, but they were given the task of organising the work platoons and seeing to our welfare and safety.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And so when you were at the frontline positions, you were guarded, I take it by members of the HVO; is that right?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN LUKOVIC
utterances.text: They guarded us in the sense of preventing us from being in the line of fire of the other side, so they would task the HVO soldiers to caution us and tell us where not to go, where to go, where to be wary of snipers, where to be wary of mortar fire. They would say if you go to have lunch you must pass along a protected zone and so on. So they indicated the hot spots, so to speak, the dangerous areas, so that we were very well-infomed and I remain standing to this day. I was not wounded, whereas there was heavy fighting going on, in Bobasi for example.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you were at the frontlines, did you see other units such as the Vitezovi at the frontlines, where you were taken to dig trenches?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN LUKOVIC
utterances.text: Where I was I did not see the Vitezovi. And when I did my digging I did not see them.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, were you considered to be part of the HVO as a member of the work platoon?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN LUKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. And in my document it states, "Member of the 92nd Home Guards Regiment." And when I received this document, this was after -- my documents after the war, I was a member and belonged to this military unit.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, when you were at these various frontline positions as a member of the work platoon, could you tell the Court how the HVO communicated with each other and how they communicated to their positions in the rear?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN LUKOVIC
utterances.text: I don't think this is within the frameworks of what I was saying. As a member of the work platoon I didn't enter into these matters, and I don't think we ought to have been informed as to communications and links. This is a military matter. We did not meddle in military matters of that kind, but quite naturally they probably did maintain communication lines, but I really didn't see any devices of that kind. I would tell you if I had. I didn't have the possibility of going there probably. And every army has a system of communications, if it is an army. If it is an army it must know how to organise itself. And later on we heard that both sides had communicating systems and lines and everything else that they needed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How was it the information was passed to your work platoon that an attack was imminent? How did the HVO receive that information, if you know, and how did they then convey that to you?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN LUKOVIC
utterances.text: I'm not aware of how they received this information, but the commander of the line came to us and told us to pick up our picks and shovels, and to return the equipment to where it came from and we should go home, because they had received information that an attack was being prepared, and then they gave us four or five soldiers to escort us, with weapons, to take to us a place of safety where a bus would be waiting for us to take us home.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: While you were at the various frontline positions that you've identified for us on the map, did you see any members of the HVO who were Muslims?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN LUKOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Are you familiar with the events at Ahmici that occurred on April 16, 1993?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN LUKOVIC
utterances.text: Only inasmuch as I was able to read in the papers, and I saw Ahmici when I went to the work -- in the work platoon to dig at Barin Gaj. That's when I saw Ahmici. And if any of us -- any of you have been there, well, the houses were is destroyed and so on, but I don't know anything else. I wasn't a participant, I just know what I read from the newspapers and so on. That's what I can tell you. Ahmici was destroyed, but there were several houses standing, and we even spent the night in one house in Ahmici, and it still has a roof and it had a couch to lie on and so on, and we slept there for one night.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And do you know about the circumstances of the destruction of Ahmici? Did you hear about that while you were either in Ahmici digging trenches or near Barin Gaj digging trenches? Did you ask the HVO soldiers what had happened?

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Mr. President, we just object to our time being used for matters that are wholly unrelated to the testimony. We don't object to the fishing but we object to our time being used. I want to make that clear.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: All right. The objection is sustained. That's outside the scope.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I should also like to ask, if possible, for you to ask me whether I was a participant. That is something that I can talk about. But anything that I read or heard about, anybody can tell you information.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Yes, you are absolutely right, Mr. Lukovic. Please change your question, Mr. Harmon.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: I will, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let me just ask one more question of you Mr. Lukovic. I just have a point of clarification. You said you were engaged in -- the translation I had was a "general purpose unit". Is that different than a work unit?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN LUKOVIC
utterances.text: In Civil Defence they have what they call these general purpose units which are regulated by law, and the law on national defence speaks of platoons. Now, these general purpose units for Civil Defence, they include the sanitary units, the anti-fire units, the units to clear up the terrain. They include work -- they are also work platoons, but in fact, work platoons or units which, for example, if there was a flood, earthquake, fire breaking out, a grenade, an explosive, to see to the town's hygiene under such conditions, to ensure heating for the population. There was done by these Civil Defence work platoons or units. And also, food had to be dispatched and handed out. When it was war, they wanted to restrict movement around Vitez because there was a lot of shelling and mortar fire and a lot of casualties. So that it was these units, these sort of work platoons, and they were the sort of general purpose units, several units, and this matter was regulated by law.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And lastly, Mr. Lukovic, how many members were there in the work platoon Kolonija?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN LUKOVIC
utterances.text: I don't know the exact number. Possibly 70, but when we went on our job it was between 15 and 25 depending on the need. The Kolonija work platoon, part it have was sent to one locality, another portion to another locality. So there would usually be between 15 and 25 of us, and they were multi-national or multi-ethnic in character the platoons.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Lukovic, thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: I've concluded my examination, Mr. President. I would ask that the map that has been marked by Mr. Lukovic, and I don't have a number, be admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Registrar, number, please?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: This will be 561.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Mr. Nobilo, do you have anything to add?

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President, but just a few questions. Re-examined by Mr. Nobilo:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Lukovic you said later on you were acquainted with members of the 92nd National Guard Regiment. When was this?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN LUKOVIC
utterances.text: This was in 1996.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And during the war it did not exist, the 92nd did not exist?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN LUKOVIC
utterances.text: No, it was just to regulate matters.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But in the war, when you were in the civil defence platoons and this -- the organisation of civil defence and the work platoons, was it under the civilian structures of the municipality?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN LUKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, the platoon I was in, in the civil defence platoons, were under civil defence authority, but the documents were issued later on in 1996.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The decision to mobilise you to a work platoon and dispatch you, who took this decision, civilian or military authorities?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN LUKOVIC
utterances.text: Exclusively the civilian authorities.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you have the possibility of going on sick leave when you were ill?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN LUKOVIC
utterances.text: I was given a 30-day sick leave period. I had a cold and various inflammations and they thought I might have jaundice as well, so I had to go for regular checkups and examinations to my physician. When the team of physicians said that I was healthy I was taken back to the work platoon. This related to all the members of the work platoon, there was always a very high level of medical care and protection, of course under the prevailing conditions.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You mentioned your work platoon Kolonija, Nadioci, Donja Veceriska; can we say that every village on the territory under HVO control had its own work platoon?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN LUKOVIC
utterances.text: I think it did, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And tell the Court, please, in view of the population structure, may we conclude that most of the members of the work platoons were Croats?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN LUKOVIC
utterances.text: We cannot say that this is true for all the work platoons.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But take an overall for the municipality.

utterances.speaker: DUSAN LUKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, overall, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Apart from the captain, all the other ranks that you saw, what were the most frequent ranks that contacted with you? What level of rank? What military ranks did these commanders hold?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN LUKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, whether they were sergeants or lance corporals, I don't know. I just mentioned the man whom I know to have held the rank of captain; but otherwise they were these people in charge of the trench and the command of 10 to 30 people, and they would assign tasks to us.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: That's all, Mr. President. That concludes the direct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Nobilo. The Judges will ask you questions now. Judge Shahabuddeen.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Mr. Lukovic, you mentioned a law which regulated the duty of people to give labour and which provided for sanctions in case they refused to do so. What was that law? When was it passed? Who passed it?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN LUKOVIC
utterances.text: At the beginning of the war the law on national defence for Bosnia-Herzegovina existed, and I think they all took it over and began to use it. But in wartime situations additional regulations were adopted concerning mobilisation. I have a quotation from the regulation concerning mobilisation and the duties of individuals, conscripts, in that regard. So, I think it was the law on national defence that was in force, because we had been organising various exercises according to that law, and probably the HVO took it over but with additional regulations. The regulation is also based on the provisions of that law, and in my time, when I was president of the municipal assembly, the same sort of work platoons existed, tied to the military component, and others tied to civil defence. There was a large scale exercise when I was mayor in the Zenica region which incorporates 12 municipalities, and I was the civilian president commanding that exercise. We also engaged these general purpose units that I mentioned earlier on, and this is how it functioned for the entire area; and therefore, I do know something about this, although many years have of course gone by and I have forgotten some of it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: You remember a great deal, and I'm grateful to you. This was, the law on national defence was a law of the central government of Bosnia-Herzegovina; do I understand you correctly? And when the HVO took power, they took over that law and applied it; is that what happened?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN LUKOVIC
utterances.text: They also passed a decree on the armed forces of the Croat community of Herceg-Bosna, and that decree exists, and it is practically a copy of that law. I mean, it was literally rewritten, that every person of military age has the duty to carry out work duty, military duty, take part in civil defence, and also in observation services. And also there are material obligations involved, and that is the same as when I was president of the municipality.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: So, the HVO would be operating that law and would be applying that law?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN LUKOVIC
utterances.text: I don't know how to answer this question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Yes or no, or qualify your answer. I repeat --

utterances.speaker: DUSAN LUKOVIC
utterances.text: The law is far broader, and I just pointed out this aspect of the armed forces related to the military obligation and work platoons, and that is why it was adjusted to the conditions involved. Also there were sanctions envisaged for those who did not carry this out, because the law did have to be adjusted. The law pertained to the Socialist Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina, and the war broke out and one had to have normative acts, laws in order to act. That is what I think, at least.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Were there people in your area who did not recognise the HVO as a legitimate authority?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN LUKOVIC
utterances.text: As far as I know, there were no such people. The territory --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Now, you went on various trench digging exercises and you were a member of groups which comprised various nationalities, including Muslims; is that right?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN LUKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Now, to your knowledge, were any of those Muslims people who had been detained at the Vitez cinema, or any of the other places where Muslims were detained?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN LUKOVIC
utterances.text: I cannot assert that; but there were some younger men who were with me on the work platoon, because I went only in June; so I imagine that there is the possibility of having such people having been there. So not from the adult education centre, but only when they went back to their homes, then they were engaged in the civil defence units and the work platoon. And the Red Cross, too, there were Muslims and Croats and Serbs there, just as in the work platoon within the military component.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: You mentioned one Muslim who rested I think on a couch, and as soon as he found an opportunity he left the area.

utterances.speaker: DUSAN LUKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: He was a member of your trench digging platoon; was he?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN LUKOVIC
utterances.text: If you are referring to this man, Topcic, he was with me, and we slept on the same couch. However, when he had an opportunity to go to Zenica, he did go. Now, for what reasons? He probably wanted to join his own people, you see, and I had no need to do that, because I had spent over 40 years there, so although I'm not a Croat, I stayed. I have no objections as far as this young man is concerned, and he worked with me at 4 or 5 different places, he and a few other men.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: While he was digging with you, did he ever protest or utter any words or show any signs of dissatisfaction?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN LUKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, he didn't show any signs of dissatisfaction towards the HVO or whatever, but vis-a-vis a situation that took us all by surprise and this senseless situation where he as a young man was forced to dig, and as we would put it in Bosnia, he tried to find a way for him to save his life, to save his head, as we would put it. He never said anything about the HVO or anything, he simply spoke of this senseless war.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: You said he was forced to dig. What would you say to this: Was it possible that there were other people who were digging trenches who were not happy with being forced to dig trenches, but who, nevertheless, thought it wise not to protest?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN LUKOVIC
utterances.text: To be quite honest, I didn't like to dig trenches, either. I'm a professor of sociology, at that time I was 58 years old. Very few people would take a pick or a shovel in that kind of rain and in weather that was even less cold than it was then, but I imagine that that's the kind of person I am, in terms of temperament, in terms of my moral views, that it was my military obligation. And that is why I took this with a feeling of responsibility, it's not that I was pleased by it or that I looked forward to it. I imagine that's the way others felt, too. But when we were there on the ground we worked hard. When we saw these young people on this side that I was on, and also there were young people on the other side, too, and perhaps all of them were workers whose director I had been. You know, this is really, it weighed on my mind, psychologically speaking, and it's a great responsibility.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: In other words, you saw it in terms of discharging your civic responsibilities as a good citizen. This was what you were required to do, and this is what you did.

utterances.speaker: DUSAN LUKOVIC
utterances.text: Exactly. And may I just add one more thing? If I were on the side of the army of Bosnia and Herzegovina, and if I had stayed there, I would have been under a military obligation there, too. And I would have accepted that, too, as my civic responsibility.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Now, if a member of your platoon were so ill-advised as to utter any words of protest and he was overheard by the guards, would any action be taken?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN LUKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, it depends on what he would say and how he would say it. But I believe that if he would protest simply by saying, "Why am I digging, what am I doing, this is senseless" I don't think he would be held responsible at all. And amongst ourselves, we did talk. And if we were assigned a task we tried to complete it as soon as possible so we would get home as soon as possible.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Suppose he were to say, "Well, I've had enough, I'm done with tools, I'm done with it" and the guards overheard him and saw what he was doing; would anything happen?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN LUKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, they would have done the same thing they would have done to me if I had said that. They wouldn't have done a thing, because that guard was not supposed to listen to what we were saying. That was not their duty. They were members of the HVO. They were holding their positions, and they were supposed to protect us, not to listen to what we were saying. So, we could have said it. And even if I would have said "I've had enough" and I wouldn't have shown up the next day, then the military police would have come to pick me up and they would have taken me to a judge, and as I said, sanctions would be imposed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Now, the judge would impose sanctions even if you said, "Well I don't want to go to that place to dig trenches because it's a dangerous area, it's too near to the frontline, and the sniper may get me." Suppose you said that to the judge; you have been a civic leader, would the judge sanction you still?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN LUKOVIC
utterances.text: If you're asking me, I wouldn't have said it, because in my statement, I mentioned that even at the frontline I was safer than in my very own home in the town of Vitez that was constantly being shelled. And this was physically strenuous, but it was safer, as I said, with the exception of Bobasi where we had withdrawn, and I said there was only one wounding and one person was just scarred. And also, in Baringaj, when I was there, the captain said to me, "Dusko, watch out, snipers are active here, so duck." And then a bullet actually went above my head. And when this same -- when this same captain went to oversee the frontline a bullet had grazed his neck, right over here (indicating). A sniper is dangerous. You can imagine how many people were killed in Vitez by sniper, over 100 citizens and children. I know that. I don't know, I wasn't at the other side, so I don't know what the situation was like over there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Do allow me to say that you would have acted in that way because of your wise judgment that perhaps it was just as safe to be digging trenches as to be at home. But you're a professor, and you would be familiar with the proposition, I take it, that two equally reasonable people could reasonably come to different conclusions on the basis of the same evidence. Suppose another equally reasonable person like you said, "No, that's too dangerous, I'm not going there"; would the judge acquit him or still convict him?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN LUKOVIC
utterances.text: I can't say. I don't know how the judge would behave. But fortunately, probably there will be no more wars, but if I were to be engaged in a work platoon again, I would go. I would go to save my family, my friends, et cetera, to fight for peace, so that later we could try to live next to each other, if nothing else, without war. Because man wants to defend himself, to defend his family, and I think that is what was done. The work platoons and our efforts, that was indispensable, so I have no objections to that, and believe me, I didn't go singing, I went there quite fearful. And you know, it was very bad for me when my son went to the frontline. His son would follow him for 50 or 100 metres and come back in tears. And I had to go. But this was a crazy war, it was a crazy war, and this is unheard of, I think, in the history of wars. That's the way it seems to me, because I've lived through the Second World War, too, but this was great psychological pressure, among other things.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Professor, I think I owe it to you to say that I've asked you the last question fully appreciating that you have not claimed to be a legally trained person, but I respect you as a civic leader, and I assume you would be acquainted with some of the elementary patterns of conduct to be expected of your judicial system. So, let me ask you one final question which arises out of your characterisation of the war as a crazy war. Would you say, Professor, that there is any prospect of these various people living in harmony with one another again?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN LUKOVIC
utterances.text: By nature I am an optimist to the bone, and I always find something bright, even in the blackest; and Muslims are coming to Vitez, they are coming to the town library, Croats are passing through Mahala, which is the Muslim part of town, they have already submitted requests for apartments and everybody is going to get his apartment back if he did have a tenant right to the apartment and if he purchases that apartment. I think that we are going to continue our relationship, perhaps not from the same point where we had stopped, but there has to be a degree of tolerance because we have to live together. In my opinion, again I'm saying it is my very own opinion, we have all lost something in this war. We are all losers in this war.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Professor, I highly respect your closing words and I thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Professor, I won't ask you many questions. The experience that you went through is a surprising one as regards service obligations. Until what age did one have these obligations, 50, 55?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN LUKOVIC
utterances.text: Up to the age of 55 men could have been mobilised and sent to serve in the armed component, and from the age of 55 to 60 they could have been engaged in work platoons. This is regulated in the decree and in the law I mentioned. However, I was a witness of what happened in Barin Gaj. Croats who were even older, 65 or 67 years of age came there as volunteers. And I'm also speaking about Nadioci. My daughter-in-law's father came and his relatives came, and they saw me and they said, "We came to help." So they were not duty bound. They were over 60 years old but they did come. But of course, if there were such people who volunteered, then they were given lighter tasks, to cut branches, to bring water, et cetera, not exactly to dig with a shovel.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: As regards yourself, were you a volunteer or were you not? That's what I didn't understand. Were you a volunteer or were you not a volunteer?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN LUKOVIC
utterances.text: I was not a volunteer and I never said that. I was a responsible citizen, a law-abiding citizen, and I accepted this because I knew that this was my duty according to the law and the civilian authorities had the right to engage me. I said very few people would have volunteered to take a shovel or a pick and to go to the frontline. But staying at the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Yes, you said that to us. Let me ask you my question Mr. Lukovic, and then you can answer it specifically. I have rarely seen -- unless I'm wrong, I have rarely seen anybody who goes to dig trenches with such goodwill, with such a concern for doing the right thing. I have another question I'd like to ask you. You did your military service as part of the JNA? I suppose you did. You're at an age, I suppose, that you did your military service.

utterances.speaker: DUSAN LUKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What was your speciality? Were you a trench digger, or were you a professor or you were a technician? What was your specialisation? All of us have a specialisation when we do our military service.

utterances.speaker: DUSAN LUKOVIC
utterances.text: I did my military service in 1955 and 1956, and I was in a special signals battalion in Novi Sad, so I was in the signal corps. Not a trench digger, but in the army one doesn't dig trenches, this is only part of -- all right. Sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you. What I don't understand very clearly is that you were -- in fact, I'm asking: You were a part of the HVO; is that correct? I think that's what you said.

utterances.speaker: DUSAN LUKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The HVO, which the accused was trying to set up in a rational way, found nothing else to suggest that you do except to dig trenches, but there were transmission problems, there were specific problems, specific education had to be-- people had to be trained in specific education, but you dug ditches without asking any questions. There was no problem for you?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN LUKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, I did not take it very hard. It was a bit strange, but it is only natural that the HVO would organise it. And Croats were there, it is only natural, because these were these key positions. It is not to say that my son -- for example, my son did not dig trenches, but together with Croats he fought at the frontlines. So there was no discrimination against him. And I didn't take it that way either. But since I had been an office holder, I was president of the municipality, and then in those days there was also the League of Communists, et cetera, so they knew about all of that, but nobody mistreated me.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What city were you the mayor of? I didn't quite catch it.

utterances.speaker: DUSAN LUKOVIC
utterances.text: Vitez.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Vitez. Couldn't the HVO find anything else to suggest to the mayor of Vitez than to dig trenches? Could you explain that initially because you were Serb?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN LUKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, yes. No. No. No, no, no. There were Croats who were also directors. There was a director of the military factory, and he was also at the frontline and there was also a Croat director who was digging trenches together with me. So no, no, no, I don't think that was the problem at all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: All right. That's all we have to say about that. I'm sure that you will agree with me when I say that bearing arms, or digging trenches or occupying other specific functions is something that seems a bit strange, that is to ask the mayor of Vitez to go to dig trenches, but I won't ask you anything else about that. You've tried to answer. I would like to ask you another question now. You did this, if not with enthusiasm, at least with a degree of goodwill. It must have been difficult for you, because I suppose you were digging trenches all day long. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN LUKOVIC
utterances.text: Not all day long. We would start around 7.00, from 7.00 to 12.00 with breaks. Naturally, one person would be digging, the other person would be taking the earth away, so you could sit down every half hour or hour, and then we would go for lunch, and then we would continue digging. I don't know, perhaps for another three or four hours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: All right. Then you found yourself in that very strange position, that is you are a member of the HVO, you're a Serb, a member of the HVO, the mayor of Vitez, you're sent to dig trenches. The thing I'm wondering about is how were you perceived within this squad in which there were Muslims? I believe it was the time of multiculturalism. Were you perceived as a double agent, or did the guards ask you to do small favours for them, or to give them information about what the Muslims were saying or not at all? You just dug trenches like everybody else?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN LUKOVIC
utterances.text: No. I told you, I lived there for 40 years and I know Croats as well as I know Muslims. They were my students, and they tried to be even fairer to me. For example, this member of the HVO would sometimes take a shovel from me and he would dig instead of me. So no, they didn't talk about spying or anything like that. I'm just talking about where I was. Where I was there were no problems. Everybody was treated very fairly, except that the work involved was not the kind of work that people liked to do, but we don't like the war either, but we had to choose between two evils, whether we would try to prevent it or have even graver consequences. But I took stoically that I was mayor, I was a director, et cetera. It was the times of war, and I thought that as soon as I got it over with the better.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: JUDGE JORDA: Well, yes. That was my last question. You considered this task one which was necessary in order to defend your country, your homeland; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN LUKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, I wouldn't say "homeland." I would say that part of Vitez, because it is relative what homeland is. My homeland is Bosnia-Herzegovina because I was born in Bosnia-Herzegovina. When this disintegration took place, then everybody fought for the territory that they were in, and then now we are going to try to rectify certain things and let us learn from our mistakes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: I see. You who are more an intellectual than a worker, even if you were in a workers' faculty, what political regime, system, seemed legitimate to you at that point? Was it the HVO that you found legitimate or was it the authorities in Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN LUKOVIC
utterances.text: It is hard for me to say who was legitimate and who was not, because there was a war going on and there were encirclements on all sides. We in Vitez had surrounded Mahala, and then the members of the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina were around our area, and then Karadzic's Serbs had encircled the Croats or the Muslims, and you did not even know who was encircling who, and we tried to make the situation more bearable and to have less casualties in the area where we lived.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: But you did take sides, did you not? When you were in the HVO you had taken sides.

utterances.speaker: DUSAN LUKOVIC
utterances.text: I took sides by remaining in Vitez. I have a family. As I said, my son, my daughter-in-law, my two grandchildren, my wife and I. We have our apartment there. My son was born in Vitez I like Vitez very much. I could have left Vitez and gone to Serbian territory, but it is not Serb territory that is my homeland, Karadzic's territory. I stayed with my friends. I have quite a few Croat friends. I have also colleagues and friends who are Muslims, colleagues from the university, et cetera. So I looked at it from another point of view. I stayed and I'm duty bound as a man, as a parent and a grandparent to defend this territory together with the Croats. Later on when peace would come and when people would sit at the negotiating table, things would be worked out.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Thank you, Professor. You have tried to answer all the questions that you were asked. The Tribunal is appreciative of that and hopes you continue to live in Vitez under conditions that match your wishes and your ideals. Thank you once again. We will now suspend the hearing for about 15 minutes and then we will resume, unless you have no further witnesses. Mr. Nobilo?

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Mr. President, we have no further witnesses for today, because we thought that the cross-examination of the previous witness would take longer. So we could bring in our next two witnesses tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Mr. President, I wish to thank you for your kind words.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Thank you. All right. We will adjourn now and we will resume tomorrow at 10.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: at 5.14 p.m., to be reconvened on Thursday, the 17th day of December, 1998 at 10.00 a.m. 23 24 25
